summary: A PTZ camera can now be told WHERE to look, not just which way to nudge. Save a position on the camera under a name you choose — Front gate, Loading bay — and send the camera there with one press, from the same place you drive it. Set a home position and send it back. Build a guard tour: an ordered route of those positions, with however long you want the camera to hold each one, running on its own and coming back after a power cut without anybody restarting it. And point a camera at trouble automatically: any detection rule can name a saved position, so a rule that spots someone at the fence swings the dome onto the gate and holds it there while somebody looks. The saved positions live ON THE CAMERA, where the camera's own web page put them, so the two can never disagree about where it can point — and if a position is deleted from the camera, the tour that used it says so instead of quietly skipping it. When three things want the same camera at once, the order is fixed and deliberate: the person at the controls always wins, because they are watching something the appliance cannot see; an alarm outranks the patrol; and the patrol runs when nobody else wants the camera. An alarm arriving while you are driving the camera is reported to you rather than taking it out of your hands. A patrol that can no longer walk its route — because its positions were deleted from the camera — stops and raises an alert, rather than reporting itself as running while nothing moves.
compatibility: Purely additive for anybody without a PTZ camera: nothing changes, and the new panel only appears on cameras that report PTZ. One behaviour worth knowing about if you use both guard tours and tamper detection: while a camera is patrolling, this appliance will not report it as re-aimed or as having a blocked lens. Those two checks work by comparing what the camera sees now against what it normally sees, and a camera that is supposed to keep changing what it looks at has no 'normally'. Without this, every patrolling camera would raise a tamper alert every few minutes. The frozen-picture check still works throughout, so a patrolling camera whose feed dies is still caught, and both checks return the moment the patrol stops. The screen says all of this while a patrol is running rather than leaving it to be discovered. Two related fixes: an alert raised by hand — including from the rule editor's own Test button — now moves the camera exactly as a real detection would, instead of notifying and doing nothing; and deleting a camera now removes its guard tours with it. Moving a camera by any route also no longer makes the tamper monitor report it as interfered with. Operators need no new permission: saving positions and running tours sit under the existing 'may move a camera' level of Live Views, which now also grants reading them — without that read an operator had the buttons and no way to see what they pointed at.
